title: CRYSTAL input and output field guide
section: What to recognize in the output
text:
What to recognize in the output

Sampling
CRYSTAL prints a line similar to:
SHRINK. FACT.(MONKH.) ... NUMBER OF K POINTS IN THE IBZ ...
This gives both the Monkhorst sampling and the number of k-points that remain after symmetry reduction to the irreducible Brillouin zone.


SCF cycles
During the self-consistent field procedure CRYSTAL prints lines beginning with:
CYC
These contain the current total energy and the change with respect to the previous cycle.


Successful SCF convergence
For this laboratory the parser requires a line containing:
SCF ENDED - CONVERGENCE ON ENERGY
The final energy printed on that line is the value analysed in the notebook.


Timing
Near the end of a normal calculation, CRYSTAL reports:
END ... TELAPSE ... TCPU ...
TELAPSE is the wall-clock time experienced by the calculation.
TCPU is accumulated CPU time. With parallel execution, CPU time and elapsed time are not expected to be identical.


Normal termination
A complete run ends with a termination marker. The course parser checks this as well as SCF convergence.
crumbs: CRYSTAL input and output field guide

title: Phonons and Quantas — Quick reference
section: Convert a CRYSTAL phonon output for Quantas
text:
Convert a CRYSTAL phonon output for Quantas
Python API:
from quantas.api import ha

ha.create_input(
    "mgo_gamma.out",
    "mgo_gamma.yaml",
    interface="crystal",
    jobname="MgO Gamma phonons",
    formula_units=1,
)
Command-line equivalent:
quantas ha inpgen mgo_gamma.out \
    --interface crystal \
    --output mgo_gamma.yaml \
    --jobname "MgO Gamma phonons"

title: Phonons and Quantas — Quick reference
text:
q-point weights
A full uniform mesh may use equal weights.
A symmetry-reduced mesh must use the correct multiplicities of the irreducible q-points.
Quantas normalizes weights by their sum and deliberately does not infer multiplicities from q-point coordinates during the HA calculation.
The laboratory helper:
irreducible_qpoint_table("mgo_2x2x2.yaml")
uses spglib and the structural information stored in the normalized Quantas input to summarize symmetry-equivalent points.

title: Phonons and Quantas — Quick reference
text:
Run harmonic thermodynamics
The course helper uses the public Quantas HA API and returns heat-capacity curves in molar units:
from mineral_science_tools.phonons import ha_cv_curve

cv = ha_cv_curve(
    "mgo_2x2x2.yaml",
    temperature_max=1200.0,
    temperature_step=10.0,
)
Quantas HA API:
https://quantas.readthedocs.io/en/2.0.0-beta/api/ha.html

The harmonic calculation produces \(C_V\).
The experimental reference plotted in Laboratory 4 is approximately \(C_P\).
The difference between them is part of the scientific interpretation, not a plotting error.

title: Laboratory 2 — From structure to energy
text:
In the first laboratory a CIF was enough to describe where the atoms are and how symmetry generates a periodic crystal. We now ask a different question:
This sounds like a request for a single number. It is not. A first-principles calculation contains both a physical model and a set of numerical approximations. Understanding the difference between them is one of the most important habits in computational mineralogy.
We will again use MgO. This is deliberate. Periclase is structurally simple, small enough that calculations are fast, and still a genuine periodic ionic solid. We can therefore concentrate on the logic of the calculation rather than on the complexity of the mineral.

title: Laboratory 2 — From structure to energy
text:
A map of the calculation
The calculation can be viewed as a sequence:
crystal structure
      ↓
electronic-structure model
      ├── basis set
      └── exchange-correlation functional
      ↓
numerical choices
      ├── reciprocal-space sampling
      ├── integral thresholds
      └── SCF convergence threshold
      ↓
self-consistent solution
      ↓
total energy
      ↓
numerical convergence test
The distinction between the two middle levels is essential.
Model accuracy asks whether the chosen physical approximation is suitable for the scientific problem. A different exchange-correlation functional, for example, defines a different approximation to the electronic problem.
Numerical convergence asks whether the chosen model has been solved accurately enough. Increasing the number of k-points does not change PBE into a better density functional; it reduces one numerical error within a PBE calculation.
A calculation can therefore be tightly converged and still disagree with experiment because the physical model is incomplete. Conversely, a sophisticated physical model can give poor results if its numerical parameters are not converged.

title: Laboratory 2 — From structure to energy
section: Density functional theory, without the machinery
text:
Density functional theory, without the machinery
The electrons in a mineral require a quantum-mechanical description. Solving the full interacting many-electron problem directly is impractical for the systems of interest here. Density functional theory (DFT) reformulates the problem around the electron density and leads to a practical set of Kohn–Sham equations that are solved iteratively.
The part of the energy associated with exchange and correlation is not known exactly for general systems and must be approximated by an exchange-correlation functional.
A useful qualitative organization is often called Jacob’s ladder:



Level
Typical family
General idea




1
LDA
depends on the local density


2
GGA
adds information on density gradients


3
meta-GGA
includes additional semilocal information


4
hybrid
mixes part of exact Hartree–Fock exchange



Going upward generally changes both the mathematical model and the computational cost. It does not mean that a higher rung is automatically better for every material and every property.
In this laboratory the functional is PBE, a GGA functional. The functional is fixed: it is not part of today’s convergence experiment.

title: Laboratory 2 — From structure to energy
section: The basis set: the language used for the orbitals
text:
The basis set: the language used for the orbitals
CRYSTAL represents crystalline orbitals using localized Gaussian basis functions centred on atoms. A basis set is therefore the numerical language used to represent the electronic wavefunctions.
A larger and more flexible basis can represent the electronic structure more accurately, but generally increases computational cost and may introduce its own numerical difficulties.
For this laboratory we use the internally available POB-TZVP-REV2 basis set. It is already selected for you. You should be able to recognize the basis-set section of the input, but you are not being asked to optimize the basis set.






NoteFixed does not mean universally optimal



PBE and POB-TZVP-REV2 are kept fixed so that we can isolate one numerical question. Their use here does not establish that this combination is the best possible model for every MgO property.

title: Laboratory 2 — From structure to energy
Laboratory 2 — From structure to energy
section: Why a periodic solid needs k-points
text:
Why a periodic solid needs k-points
The electronic states of a periodic crystal are described in reciprocal space. In principle, quantities involving the electronic structure require integration over the Brillouin zone. Numerically, this integral is replaced by a finite set of k-points.
CRYSTAL uses the SHRINK keyword to construct a commensurate Monkhorst–Pack-type grid. For the cubic MgO calculation used here, a value \(IS\) corresponds to a nominal sampling based on reciprocal-lattice increments
\[
\frac{\mathbf{b}_1}{IS},\qquad
\frac{\mathbf{b}_2}{IS},\qquad
\frac{\mathbf{b}_3}{IS}.
\]
It is therefore convenient to think of the sequence as increasingly dense nominal \(IS\times IS\times IS\) grids.
This does not mean that CRYSTAL diagonalizes the Kohn–Sham matrix at \(IS^3\) independent points. Crystal symmetry reduces the sampling to the irreducible Brillouin zone (IBZ), and the output reports the actual number of irreducible k-points used.
Increasing SHRINK therefore changes two things that we can observe directly:

the numerical approximation to Brillouin-zone integration;
the computational work required by the calculation.

Running the calculation on CluMiner
CRYSTAL is licensed software and is run on the university cluster, not inside Codespaces.
For this laboratory the standard submission command is:
cluminer-crystal mgo_shrink2.d12 --cores-per-node 2 --threads 2
The same resource request must be used for every calculation in the convergence series. With these settings the launcher uses one MPI rank with two OpenMP threads.
Keeping the hardware request fixed is important: if the computational resources changed from one calculation to another, timing comparisons would be much less informative.

title: Laboratory 2 — From structure to energy
Laboratory 2 — From structure to energy
text:
Energy convergence
For a sequence ordered by increasing SHRINK, the notebook calculates the change relative to the preceding sampling:
\[
\Delta E_i = E_i-E_{i-1}.
\]
Because the sign is not important for the convergence criterion, we will normally inspect
\[
|\Delta E_i|.
\]
The same value is expressed in hartree and in kJ mol\(^{-1}\) of MgO.
For this CRYSTAL model the primitive computational cell contains one MgO formula unit, so the conversion can be interpreted directly per mole of MgO:
\[
1\ E_\mathrm{h} \approx 2625.5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.
\]
The notebook calculates the conversion from physical constants rather than asking you to perform it manually.

title: Laboratory 2 — From structure to energy
section: Convergence is a decision, not a magic number
text:
Convergence is a decision, not a magic number
The densest calculation is not automatically the best practical choice.
As SHRINK increases, the energy should become progressively less sensitive to further refinement, while computational cost generally increases. Your task is to choose a sampling that is sufficiently converged for the purpose of the subsequent calculations without paying for unnecessary numerical precision.
Values such as \(0.1\) or \(0.01\) kJ mol\(^{-1}\) can be useful scales when looking at the table, but they are not universal laws. The necessary precision depends on the scientific question. Resolving a very small phase-energy difference may require a tighter criterion than obtaining a preliminary equilibrium structure.
The final question of the laboratory is therefore not:

What is the largest SHRINK value?

but:

Which SHRINK value would you carry forward, and why is its balance between numerical stability and computational cost adequate?

That decision will matter in the next activity, when the geometry of MgO is allowed to change.

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
A crystal structure is often first encountered as a picture: coloured spheres, polyhedra, chains, layers or frameworks. The picture is useful, but it is not the structure itself. A crystallographic model is a compact mathematical description of a periodic arrangement. In this laboratory we will start from that description and reconstruct the structure step by step.
The practical question is simple:
This is the first computational activity because it establishes a workflow that will return throughout the course: a structural model is read from data, analysed, visualized, checked against symmetry, and eventually used as the starting point for calculations of energy and physical properties.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
section: The CIF as a crystallographic description
text:
The CIF as a crystallographic description
The Crystallographic Information File (CIF) is a structured text format. For the present exercise, the most important information is the unit cell, the space group, the atomic sites, their fractional coordinates and their occupancies.
The fractional coordinate \((x,y,z)\) does not give a distance in ångström. Instead, it gives a position relative to the three direct-lattice vectors \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{b}\), and \(\mathbf{c}\):
\[
\mathbf{r} = x\mathbf{a} + y\mathbf{b} + z\mathbf{c}.
\]
This is why the same fractional coordinates can describe geometrically different Cartesian positions when the cell parameters change.
A CIF normally does not need to list every atom that appears in a conventional unit cell. It can store only the crystallographically independent sites. The remaining sites follow from the symmetry of the space group.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
Asymmetric unit and unit cell
The asymmetric unit is the smallest part of the structure from which the contents of the unit cell can be generated by applying the appropriate space-group operations. The unit cell, in turn, generates the infinite periodic crystal by translation.
This distinction is easy to lose when looking only at a structure drawing. MgO provides a particularly clean example. Only one Mg site and one O site are needed in its crystallographic description, but applying the symmetry and centring operations generates the complete contents of the conventional cubic cell.
In the notebook we therefore inspect the structure twice: first as the list of sites written in the CIF, and then as the symmetry-expanded unit cell. The difference between these lists is itself part of the crystallographic information.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
Two complementary symmetry tools
We use Gemmi and spglib for different reasons.
Gemmi is used to read the CIF as a crystallographic document. It understands the unit cell, space-group symbols, symmetry operations and atomic sites. In other words, it can tell us what crystallographic information the file claims to contain.
spglib approaches the problem from another direction. We give it lattice vectors, atomic coordinates and atomic species. It then searches numerically for operations that map the structure onto itself. This requires a tolerance, because coordinates in real structure files are finite-precision numbers and experimental structures are never mathematical abstractions with infinitely exact coordinates.
The comparison is useful:
\[
\text{symmetry stated in the CIF}
\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{symmetry implied by the numerical structure}.
\]
Agreement is a consistency check. Disagreement is not something to hide by changing parameters until the desired answer appears. It is a result that must be understood: the structure may be distorted, the tolerance may be inappropriate, the CIF may use a non-standard setting, or the structural model may contain disorder or partial occupancies.
For this first exercise we use ordered structures with full occupancies so that the symmetry analysis remains unambiguous.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
Symmetry operations in coordinate form
A space-group operation can be written as a transformation of fractional coordinates. The identity is
\[
(x,y,z)\rightarrow(x,y,z),
\]
whereas an operation written, for example, as
-y,x,z
maps
\[
(x,y,z)\rightarrow(-y,x,z).
\]
Translations may appear as fractional additions such as \(1/2\). Rather than printing every operation of a high-symmetry space group without context, the notebook first shows a compact set of Hall-derived operations and the lattice centring translations, and then lets you inspect part of the full operation list.
The software can describe the matrix and translational parts of an operation, but interpreting an operation geometrically remains a crystallographic task. In particular, the presence of a translational component is what distinguishes operations such as screw axes and glide planes from their purely point-symmetry counterparts.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
Wyckoff positions
The atoms of a crystal can also be organized into Wyckoff positions. A Wyckoff position identifies an orbit of symmetrically equivalent points in a given space group.
Three pieces of information are especially useful:

the multiplicity, which gives the number of equivalent sites in the conventional unit cell;
the Wyckoff letter, which distinguishes inequivalent orbits;
the site symmetry, which describes the subgroup of operations that leaves a particular site invariant.

A multiplicity is therefore not the number of independent atoms that had to be entered in the CIF. Quite the opposite: several atoms in the conventional cell may all be generated from one crystallographically independent site.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
Visualization is inspection, not proof
The notebooks use py3Dmol to display the CIF interactively. You can rotate the structure, zoom, draw the unit-cell box and replicate the cell to make periodicity easier to see.
The default representation uses spheres without automatically inferred bonds. This choice is deliberate. A line drawn between two atoms by a visualization program is based on a graphical or distance criterion; it is not itself a crystallographic observable and should not silently determine how we interpret bonding in a mineral.
The viewer is therefore an aid to scientific inspection. The quantitative description still comes from the crystallographic data and symmetry analysis.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

MgO is useful because the rocksalt structure is simple enough that the relationship between asymmetric unit, face-centred cell, symmetry and Wyckoff multiplicity remains visible.
You will then receive a second CIF and repeat the same reasoning independently in:

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
text:
The structure used in an electronic-structure calculation usually comes from experiment. That is an excellent place to begin, but it is not automatically the equilibrium structure of the computational model.
This distinction is easy to overlook. A CIF describes a structure observed under particular experimental conditions. The static DFT calculation used in this laboratory describes a different idealized situation: the electronic ground-state energy of a periodic crystal within a chosen functional and basis set, without thermal expansion and without vibrational free-energy contributions.
Laboratory 3 therefore begins by asking:
Once that minimum has been found, we deliberately move away from it and ask:
The answer leads directly to an equation of state and to one of the most important mechanical properties of a mineral: the bulk modulus.
crumbs: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
text:
Why optimize an experimental structure?
Suppose that an experimental CIF gives a cell parameter \(a_\mathrm{exp}\) and a set of atomic coordinates. If we evaluate the DFT energy at that geometry, we obtain a perfectly valid energy for that particular configuration. But the geometry is not guaranteed to minimize the energy of our computational model.
Several reasons contribute to this.
First, an experimental lattice parameter is normally measured at a finite temperature, often close to ambient conditions. Thermal expansion is therefore already present in the observation. Our present calculation is a static electronic-structure calculation. It does not yet contain the vibrational free energy responsible for finite-temperature expansion, and it does not include zero-point vibrational effects unless they are added explicitly later.
Second, the chosen density functional and basis set define an approximate energy surface. Even at exactly \(0\) K and zero external pressure, their predicted equilibrium geometry need not coincide perfectly with experiment.
The purpose of geometry optimization is therefore not to “correct” the experiment. It is to find the structure that is internally consistent with the computational model we have chosen.
crumbs: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
section: Forces, stress and the minimum-energy structure
text:
Forces, stress and the minimum-energy structure
For a periodic crystal, geometry may involve both:

internal degrees of freedom, describing atomic positions within the cell;
cell degrees of freedom, describing lattice parameters and cell shape.

At equilibrium, the gradient of the energy with respect to every allowed degree of freedom should vanish within the selected numerical tolerances.
Atomic forces are related to derivatives of the energy with respect to atomic coordinates:
\[
\mathbf{F}_i =
-\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}.
\]
The stress tensor plays the corresponding role for deformation of the unit cell. If no external pressure or stress is applied, the equilibrium cell is the one for which the residual internal stress vanishes within the numerical accuracy of the calculation.
This distinction matters particularly for MgO.
crumbs: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
section: Why MgO is an unusually clean example
text:
Why MgO is an unusually clean example
Periclase has the rocksalt structure, space group \(Fm\bar{3}m\). Mg and O occupy special symmetry positions. Their fractional coordinates are fixed by the space-group symmetry.
This has an interesting consequence: the atomic forces may already vanish by symmetry even when the lattice parameter is not the equilibrium one.
The structure can therefore require a geometry optimization without any atomic coordinate moving at all. What changes is the unit cell, driven by its residual stress.
This is a useful reminder that
zero atomic forces
does not necessarily mean
fully optimized periodic crystal.
The cell itself may still be away from equilibrium.
crumbs: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
text:
Full geometry optimization in CRYSTAL
CRYSTAL performs geometry optimization through the OPTGEOM block. In this laboratory we use:
OPTGEOM
FULLOPTG
...
END
FULLOPTG allows optimization of both the cell and the internal coordinates that are permitted by symmetry.
The optimization is stopped when numerical criteria on the gradient, displacement and energy change are satisfied.
For the course calculation we use:
TOLDEG = 0.0004
TOLDEX = 0.0001
TOLDEE = 10^-8
The first two are criteria on the RMS gradient and RMS displacement, respectively; TOLDEE controls the energy difference between optimization steps.
These are numerical stopping conditions. They do not define the physical model and they do not make the DFT approximation itself more accurate.
The CRYSTAL23 manual documents FULLOPTG, CVOLOPT, TOLDEG, TOLDEX and TOLDEE in the OPTGEOM input block:
https://www.crystal.unito.it/documentation.html
crumbs: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
text:
Which cell is CRYSTAL printing?
MgO provides another useful crystallographic trap.
The familiar crystallographic description is a conventional cubic face-centred cell with one cubic lattice parameter \(a\).
A primitive cell of the same FCC lattice can instead be described by three equal vectors separated by \(60^\circ\). Its numerical cell parameters therefore look very different even though it represents exactly the same infinite crystal.
CRYSTAL may print different cell representations in different parts of an output. When a cell no longer “looks cubic”, do not immediately conclude that the cubic symmetry has been lost. First identify whether you are looking at a primitive or crystallographic representation.
That distinction will return when Quantas normalizes energy–volume data.
crumbs: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
section: From one equilibrium point to a compression curve
text:
From one equilibrium point to a compression curve
Once the static equilibrium geometry is known, we can investigate how the crystal responds to changes in volume.
Experimentally, high-pressure mineral physics often approaches this problem using X-ray diffraction in a diamond-anvil cell. Pressure is applied to the sample and the evolution of its lattice parameters and volume is measured.
A static electronic-structure calculation can approach the same constitutive behaviour from a complementary direction. Instead of physically applying a pressure, we calculate a set of structures at selected volumes and evaluate their energies.
This produces an energy–volume path:
\[
E(V).
\]
The pressure associated with that path is obtained from the derivative
\[
P(V) =
-\frac{dE}{dV}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
E(V)-E(V_\mathrm{ref})
=
-\int_{V_\mathrm{ref}}^{V} P(V')\,dV'.
\]
This is why an energy–volume calculation contains the information needed to reconstruct a static pressure–volume relation.
crumbs: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
section: What is an equation of state?
crumbs: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
section: Bulk modulus: how difficult is the crystal to compress?
text:
Bulk modulus: how difficult is the crystal to compress?
The isothermal bulk modulus is defined as
\[
K =
-V\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial V}\right)_T.
\]
At the equilibrium volume,
\[
K_0 =
-V_0
\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial V}\right)_{V_0}.
\]
A large bulk modulus means that a large pressure change is required to produce a given fractional change in volume: the material is relatively incompressible. A smaller bulk modulus corresponds to a more compressible material.
In the present calculation \(K_0\) is a static bulk modulus derived from the DFT energy surface. Temperature-dependent experimental values need not be identical.
crumbs: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
text:
Why constant-volume optimization?
To construct an EOS we need the minimum energy at each selected volume.
If we simply changed the volume and then performed another completely free FULLOPTG calculation, every point would attempt to return to the same equilibrium volume. We would destroy the independent variable of the experiment.
CRYSTAL therefore provides:
CVOLOPT
for full geometry optimization at constant volume.
The logic is:
choose V
   ↓
keep V fixed
   ↓
relax all structural degrees of freedom
that remain allowed
   ↓
obtain the minimum E compatible with V
For a lower-symmetry mineral this may involve genuine changes in cell shape and internal coordinates.
For cubic MgO the situation is particularly simple. At fixed volume the cubic symmetry fixes the cell shape, and the Mg and O coordinates are fixed by their special positions. Almost no structural freedom remains. A constant-volume optimization may therefore converge essentially immediately.
That apparently trivial result is itself instructive:

symmetry determines which structural degrees of freedom exist.
crumbs: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
text:
Choosing the volume series
The reference volume is the volume of the optimized static structure, \(V_0\).
We use the factors
\[
\frac{V}{V_0}
=
0.91,\;
0.94,\;
0.97,\;
1.00,\;
1.03,\;
1.06,\;
1.09.
\]
For a cubic crystal,
\[
V=a^3.
\]
Therefore the lattice parameter cannot be scaled by the same numerical factor as the volume. For a target volume factor \(f\),
\[
a(f)=a_0 f^{1/3}.
\]
This cube-root relation matters. Setting \(a=0.91a_0\) would not give \(V=0.91V_0\); it would give
\[
V=(0.91)^3V_0 \approx 0.754V_0,
\]
which is a much stronger compression.
The notebook calculates the correct target lattice parameters for you.
crumbs: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
text:
The role of Quantas
The EOS analysis is performed with Quantas 2.0.
Quantas can read a list of CRYSTAL outputs, normalize their structural and energetic information consistently, generate an energy–volume dataset and fit an integrated EOS. For this laboratory we ask it to express the results in the conventional crystallographic cell, which makes the fitted cubic lattice parameter directly comparable with the MgO cell used in the course.
The Quantas energy–volume workflow reconstructs pressure from the fitted energy relation using
\[
P(V)=-\frac{dE}{dV}.
\]
The current MgO energy–volume tutorial in the Quantas documentation uses the same type of seven-point CRYSTAL dataset and a BM3 fit:
https://quantas.readthedocs.io/en/2.0.0-beta/tutorials/eos_ev.html
The software performs the repetitive numerical work. Your task is to decide whether the data and fitted parameters make physical sense.
crumbs: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state

title: Laboratory 3 — From equilibrium structure to an equation of state
text:
The complete workflow
The activity follows one continuous chain:
experimental MgO structure
        ↓
full static geometry optimization
        ↓
DFT equilibrium structure
        ↓
choose V/V0 values
        ↓
constant-volume calculations
        ↓
E(V) dataset
        ↓
BM3 fit
        ↓
V0, K0, K'0
        ↓
P(V) and interpretation
This is the first laboratory in which a sequence of electronic-structure calculations becomes a macroscopic mineral property.

title: Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
text:
In the previous laboratories we treated a crystal first as a structure, then as an electronic-energy problem, and finally as a mechanically compressible solid. Temperature has so far played almost no role.
This laboratory introduces the missing microscopic ingredient: lattice vibrations.
The objective is not simply to calculate a list of frequencies. We want to follow the complete chain
and then compare those predictions with experiment.
That comparison is deliberately expected to be imperfect. By the end of the laboratory you should be able to distinguish a discrepancy caused by insufficient q-point sampling from one caused by the harmonic approximation itself.

title: Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
section: From the potential-energy surface to normal modes
text:
From the potential-energy surface to normal modes
After Laboratory 3, MgO is at a stationary geometry of the static DFT energy surface. Close to that minimum, the energy can be expanded in the atomic displacements \(\mathbf{u}\):
\[
E(\mathbf{u})
\simeq
E_0
+
\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm T}
\mathbf{H}
\mathbf{u}.
\]
\(\mathbf{H}\) is the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives of the energy with respect to atomic displacements.
Stopping the expansion at second order defines the harmonic approximation. The potential-energy surface is locally replaced by a multidimensional quadratic surface. After mass weighting and diagonalization, the coupled atomic motions become independent normal modes with characteristic frequencies.
For an isolated molecule this would already give a finite set of molecular vibrations. A crystal contains an additional ingredient: translational periodicity.

title: Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
section: A phonon has both a branch and a wave vector
text:
A phonon has both a branch and a wave vector
A periodic crystal can sustain collective vibrations in which equivalent cells do not all move with the same phase. A phonon mode is therefore labelled not only by a branch index \(j\), but also by a wave vector \(\mathbf{q}\):
\[
\nu_{\mathbf{q}j}.
\]
The allowed \(\mathbf{q}\) vectors are described in reciprocal space, and the non-redundant reciprocal-space domain is the first Brillouin zone.
For primitive MgO there are two atoms in the primitive cell, so the phonon spectrum contains
\[
3N = 6
\]
branches at every \(\mathbf{q}\):

three acoustic branches;
three optical branches.

The frequencies of these branches vary across the Brillouin zone. This variation is the phonon dispersion.

title: Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
section: Why the Γ point is special
text:
Why the Γ point is special
The centre of the first Brillouin zone is
\[
\Gamma:\qquad \mathbf{q}=0.
\]
At \(\Gamma\), equivalent unit cells oscillate in phase.
A \(\Gamma\)-point phonon calculation is not useless or merely incomplete data. It answers a very important experimental question. In ordinary first-order infrared and Raman spectroscopy, the momentum carried by the photon is tiny compared with the dimensions of a crystal Brillouin zone. Crystal-momentum conservation therefore selects phonons very close to \(\mathbf{q}=0\).
This is why calculated \(\Gamma\)-point optical frequencies can be compared with IR and Raman spectra, subject to the appropriate selection rules.
Not every \(\Gamma\) mode is automatically Raman or IR active. Activity depends on symmetry and on how the vibration couples to the electromagnetic field. Nevertheless, the relevant vibrational frequencies for first-order optical spectroscopy are \(\Gamma\)-point frequencies.
This gives \(\Gamma\) two very different roles in this laboratory:

it is physically important for spectroscopy;
it is generally insufficient for bulk thermodynamics.

Understanding why those statements are simultaneously true is one of the main objectives of the activity.

title: Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
section: Why Γ alone is not enough for thermodynamics
text:
Why Γ alone is not enough for thermodynamics
Thermodynamic properties depend on the population of the vibrational states available throughout the crystal.
In the harmonic approximation, a property can be written schematically as a weighted sum over all phonon branches and q-points:
\[
X(T)
=
\frac{1}{\sum_{\mathbf q}w_{\mathbf q}}
\sum_{\mathbf q}
w_{\mathbf q}
\sum_j
X_{\mathbf qj}(T).
\]
The precise oscillator expressions are implemented by Quantas. You are not expected to memorize them. The important information flow is
frequency ν(q,j)
      +
q-point integration weight
      +
temperature
      ↓
thermodynamic contribution
The failure of a \(\Gamma\)-only thermodynamic calculation is especially clear for the acoustic branches.
At exactly \(\Gamma\), the three acoustic modes correspond to rigid translations and have frequencies that ideally approach zero. Away from \(\Gamma\) their frequencies increase continuously. Those finite-q acoustic states are a major part of the low-frequency phonon spectrum and dominate the low-temperature heat capacity.
A calculation that contains only \(\Gamma\) therefore misses the dispersion of the acoustic branches almost completely.
This is very different from spectroscopy: the same \(\Gamma\) calculation can contain useful IR/Raman optical frequencies while remaining a very poor sampling of the vibrational states needed for thermodynamics.

title: Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
text:
Direct-space supercells and reciprocal-space sampling
CRYSTAL uses a direct-space approach to phonon dispersion calculations.
With SCELPHONO, an integer supercell is constructed from the primitive cell. For the isotropic supercells used here,
1×1×1
2×2×2
3×3×3
4×4×4
the corresponding commensurate reciprocal-space meshes contain



direct-space sampling
full q-point mesh




\(1\times1\times1\)
1


\(2\times2\times2\)
8


\(3\times3\times3\)
27


\(4\times4\times4\)
64



The relation is reciprocal: increasing the range represented in direct space allows a denser set of exactly commensurate q-points in reciprocal space.
The CRYSTAL phonon-dispersion workflow uses SCELPHONO in the geometry section and DISPERSI inside FREQCALC. The official CRYSTAL tutorial uses exactly this construction for convergence of thermodynamic properties:
https://tutorials.crystalsolutions.eu/tutorial.html?td=dispersion&tf=dispersion-ht

title: Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
section: Why CRYSTAL prints 8, 27 or 64 frequency sets
text:
Why CRYSTAL prints 8, 27 or 64 frequency sets
For the calculations used in this laboratory, CRYSTAL explicitly prints a frequency spectrum for every point of the full commensurate q mesh.
Thus a \(4\times4\times4\) calculation contains 64 q-point spectra.
At first sight this looks wasteful because many q-points are related by crystal symmetry. For thermodynamic integration there are two mathematically equivalent ways to represent the sampling.
A full uniform mesh can be written as
\[
\frac{1}{N_q}
\sum_{\mathbf q}^{N_q}
X(\mathbf q).
\]
Alternatively, symmetry-equivalent q-points can be grouped into irreducible representatives:
\[
\frac{1}{\sum_i w_i}
\sum_i
w_i X(\mathbf q_i),
\]
where \(w_i\) is the multiplicity of representative \(\mathbf q_i\).
The second form is what you may have encountered in codes such as Phonopy.

What we do in this course
Quantas can use the full CRYSTAL mesh directly. Equal weights are correct for a complete uniform mesh, and Quantas normalizes all supplied q-point weights by their sum.
For inspection, the course tools can also use spglib to group the full mesh into symmetry-equivalent sets and report an irreducible q-point table with multiplicity weights.
The weights are derived from crystal symmetry, not guessed from similar frequencies. Similar spectra are then used only as a consistency check that symmetry-related q-points really do carry equivalent vibrational information.
This distinction is important. An incorrect q-point weight changes every integrated vibrational property even if the YAML file itself remains perfectly valid.
Quantas deliberately does not invent missing multiplicities from q-point coordinates during an HA/QHA calculation. Weight provenance is part of the scientific input:
https://quantas.readthedocs.io/en/2.0.0-beta/formats/phonon_yaml.html

title: Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
text:
Heat capacity and q-point convergence
Heat capacity is particularly useful for this laboratory because its physical limits are easy to interpret.
At low temperature, only low-frequency states are populated. The acoustic phonons close to \(\Gamma\) are therefore especially important. A poor q mesh has very few points in this region, and the low-temperature heat capacity is highly sensitive to sampling.
For a three-dimensional crystal with ordinary acoustic dispersion, the low-temperature behaviour approaches the Debye form
\[
C_V \propto T^3.
\]
At high temperature, every harmonic vibrational degree of freedom approaches its classical limit. For a crystal with \(n\) atoms per chemical formula unit,
\[
C_V \longrightarrow 3nR.
\]
MgO has two atoms per formula unit, so
\[
C_V
\longrightarrow
6R
\approx
49.9\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}.
\]
This is the Dulong–Petit limit for the harmonic heat capacity of MgO.
The progression
Γ → 2×2×2 → 3×3×3 → 4×4×4
should therefore be interpreted as a numerical convergence experiment on the Brillouin-zone integral.
The question is not whether 64 q-points are intrinsically “correct”. The question is whether further refinement changes the observable by an amount that matters for the scientific interpretation.

title: Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
text:
Comparison with experimental heat capacity
The workspace contains a small experimental reference dataset for MgO.
Low-temperature values come from the measurements of Barron, Berg and Morrison compiled in the NIST Structural Ceramics Database. Higher-temperature values come from an evaluated calorimetric MgO dataset in the same NIST database.
The comparison is intentionally not between identical thermodynamic quantities.
The harmonic calculation provides
\[
C_V,
\]
the heat capacity at constant volume.
Experimental calorimetry on a solid under approximately ambient pressure is normally interpreted as a constant-pressure heat capacity,
\[
C_P.
\]
At sufficiently low temperature the difference is small. At higher temperature, thermal expansion makes the distinction increasingly important.
This is not an inconvenience to hide. It is part of the laboratory.

title: Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
section: The central limitation of the harmonic approximation
text:
The central limitation of the harmonic approximation
In the harmonic approximation used here, the frequencies are calculated at one fixed equilibrium structure. They do not change when temperature changes.
Consequently the harmonic model has no mechanism for thermal expansion:
\[
\alpha_V=0.
\]
Within that fixed-volume harmonic description,
\[
C_P=C_V.
\]
A real crystal expands with temperature, and its phonon spectrum changes as the volume changes. The real constant-pressure heat capacity therefore contains a contribution that our present HA calculation cannot reproduce.
Even after the \(3\times3\times3\) and \(4\times4\times4\) results become numerically indistinguishable, a discrepancy with experiment may remain.
That residual difference can contain several contributions:

the fixed-volume harmonic approximation;
the experimental \(C_P\) versus calculated \(C_V\) distinction;
the volume dependence of phonon frequencies;
explicit anharmonic interactions between phonons;
residual DFT/basis-set model error;
experimental uncertainty and sample differences.

The first two are particularly important for interpreting this laboratory.

title: Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
section: Numerical convergence is not physical exactness
text:
Numerical convergence is not physical exactness
This returns us to a distinction already encountered in Laboratory 2.
A \(4\times4\times4\) phonon calculation may be numerically converged with respect to q-point sampling.
That does not mean the underlying physical model has become exact.
The logic is:
Γ
↓
large q-sampling error

2×2×2
↓
smaller q-sampling error

3×3×3
↓
small q-sampling error

4×4×4
↓
q-point convergence

still different from experiment?
↓
look at the physical approximations
This is the scientific conclusion of the laboratory, not a failure of the calculation.

title: Laboratory 4 — From phonons to thermodynamics
section: Looking ahead: beyond the harmonic approximation
text:
Looking ahead: beyond the harmonic approximation
If time permits, a later activity can extend the calculation to the quasi-harmonic approximation (QHA).
The QHA repeats harmonic phonon calculations at different volumes. Frequencies then become functions of volume,
\[
\nu_{\mathbf qj}=\nu_{\mathbf qj}(V),
\]
allowing the free-energy minimum to move with temperature. Thermal expansion and the distinction between \(C_P\) and \(C_V\) then emerge naturally.
Quantas describes this extension explicitly:
https://quantas.readthedocs.io/en/2.0.0-beta/theory/qha.html
That possible extension is not required for Laboratory 4. Here the goal is first to understand what the harmonic model can predict, how its reciprocal- space sampling converges, and where its physical limits appear in comparison with experiment.

title: Computational Mineralogy Laboratory
text:
This website contains the instructions and supporting material for the computational laboratory activities of the Mineral Science course.
The laboratory environment is intentionally split into three parts:

title: Computational Mineralogy Laboratory
CRYSTAL geometry and EOS keywords
text: This page is a quick reference for the geometry-optimization keywords used in Laboratory 3. For the scientific explanation, read the Laboratory 3 page.

title: CRYSTAL geometry and EOS keywords
text:
Full geometry optimization
OPTGEOM
FULLOPTG
TOLDEG
0.0004
TOLDEX
0.0001
TOLDEE
8
PRINTFORCES
END
FULLOPTG allows optimization of both cell and symmetry-allowed internal coordinates.
TOLDEG controls the RMS gradient criterion.
TOLDEX controls the RMS displacement criterion.
TOLDEE 8 corresponds to an optimization energy-change threshold of \(10^{-8}\) hartree.
PRINTFORCES requests additional atomic-gradient information.

title: CRYSTAL geometry and EOS keywords
text:
Constant-volume optimization
For an EOS point:
OPTGEOM
CVOLOPT
TOLDEG
0.0004
TOLDEX
0.0001
TOLDEE
8
END
CVOLOPT keeps the volume fixed while relaxing any other structural degrees of freedom allowed by symmetry.

title: CRYSTAL geometry and EOS keywords
section: Why the two calculations are different
text:
Why the two calculations are different
A free geometry optimization asks:

What volume and structure minimize the energy?

A constant-volume optimization asks:

At this specified volume, what structure has the lowest energy?

The second question is the one required for an energy–volume EOS dataset.

title: Save, sync and stop
text:
Saving a notebook and saving your work to GitHub are not the same operation.
This distinction is important.
Your GitHub repository is the safety copy that should survive beyond the lifetime of an individual Codespace.

title: Save, sync and stop
text:
Save your files
Save notebooks and other edited files normally with File → Save or Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on macOS).
A saved file is safe when a Codespace is merely stopped and restarted, but it has not yet been transferred to your GitHub repository.

title: Save, sync and stop
text:
Commit your work
Open Source Control using the branch-shaped icon in the left activity bar.
You will see the files that have changed.

Stage the relevant files using the + button.
Enter a short but meaningful commit message, for example:
Complete Lab 1 symmetry analysis
Select Commit.

For routine laboratory work it is acceptable to stage all files that belong to the current activity.






WarningIf you see “Publish Branch”



Your personal workspace should already be connected to a GitHub repository.
If Source Control asks you to Publish Branch instead of allowing you to synchronize normally, you may have opened a Codespace directly from the template rather than from your personal repository. Stop and ask the instructor before continuing.

title: Save, sync and stop
text:
Synchronize with GitHub
After committing, select Sync Changes.
If GitHub asks you to confirm the synchronization, accept the operation.
Then open your repository on GitHub in a normal browser tab and verify that your latest notebook or file is visible there.
This simple check is especially useful during the first laboratory.

title: Working in Codespaces
text: A GitHub Codespace is a remote Linux computer that you control through a browser-based Visual Studio Code interface. The interface contains many tools, but only a small subset is needed for this course.

title: Working in Codespaces
section: The four areas you will use
text:
The four areas you will use
Explorer
The file icon in the left activity bar. Use it to open notebooks and files and to navigate between course/ and work/.
Notebook editor
Opening an .ipynb file displays a Jupyter notebook. Run cells with the triangular Run button or with Shift+Enter. If you are asked to select a kernel, choose the Python environment provided by the Codespace.
Terminal
Open it with Terminal → New Terminal. Course commands such as update-course and start-lab are run here.
Source Control
The branch-shaped icon in the left activity bar. Use it to commit your work and synchronize it with GitHub.

title: Working in Codespaces
text:
Reopening your existing Codespace
After the first session, do not create a new Codespace every time.
You can reopen the existing one from either:

your personal workspace repository → Code → Codespaces; or
https://github.com/codespaces.

Starting an existing stopped Codespace is normally much faster than creating a new one.

title: Working in Codespaces
text:
Where to work
The workspace follows a simple rule:
course/   instructor-controlled material
work/     your personal work
Your notebooks and answers belong under directories such as:
work/lab01/
work/lab02/
Do not use course/ as a working directory. New or corrected course material may replace files there.

title: Working in Codespaces
text:
Uploading a local file
Some laboratories may ask you to upload a CIF file or a CRYSTAL output from your own computer.
Navigate to the appropriate directory under work/ in the Explorer and drag the local file into the Explorer. Check that the file appears in the intended directory before continuing.

title: Working in Codespaces
text:
Downloading a file
To copy a result from the Codespace to your computer, right-click the file in the Explorer and select Download.

title: Working in Codespaces
text:
A few useful terminal commands
You only need a very small amount of Linux for the notebook part of the course:
pwd
shows the current directory.
ls
lists files and directories.
cd work/lab01
moves into a directory.
cd ..
moves one level upward.
These are simply tools used to inspect and analyse mineral-science data.
Continue with Save, sync and stop.

title: How the laboratory works
text:
The computational laboratory uses a browser-based working environment so that all students can use the same scientific software without installing and configuring Python packages locally.
The working environment has three separate components.
The course website and your workspace are deliberately separate. You should not duplicate this website repository. Instead, you will create your own private repository from the dedicated Mineral Science workspace template.

title: How the laboratory works
text:
Your personal workspace
Your workspace repository contains two directories with very different roles:
course/
work/
course/ contains material distributed by the teacher. It may be updated during the course.
work/ contains your work: notebooks, answers, uploaded data, figures and processed results.






ImportantOne rule prevents most problems



Do not edit files directly inside course/. Work inside work/.


When a new laboratory is released, the usual workflow is:
update-course
      ↓
start-lab NN
      ↓
work/labNN/
      ↓
save → commit → sync
      ↓
stop Codespace
You do not need to understand Git internals to use this workflow. The necessary operations are introduced in the following pages.

title: Assignment 2 — From structure to energy
text:
In Laboratory 2 we will perform our first electronic-structure calculations with CRYSTAL23. We will continue to use MgO (periclase), so that the structure remains simple while we concentrate on a new question:
You are not expected to learn electronic-structure theory or the CRYSTAL input language in full. The aim is to understand the logic of a first-principles calculation, recognize the important parts of an input and output file, and perform a controlled convergence test.

title: Assignment 2 — From structure to energy
text:
Before the laboratory
Read:

Laboratory 2 — From structure to energy;
the short CRYSTAL input and output field guide;
the CluMiner quick reference.

Then update your personal workspace:
update-course
and create the Laboratory 2 working directory:
start-lab 02
Open:
work/lab02/
You should find:
01-first-scf.ipynb
02-kpoint-convergence.ipynb
inputs/
outputs/
reference-results/
The first notebook is guided. The second contains the convergence activity and your answers.






ImportantKeep the numerical experiment controlled



During the convergence test you will change only the SHRINK factor.
The MgO structure, basis set, exchange-correlation functional, integral thresholds, SCF convergence threshold and computational resources must remain unchanged.

title: Assignment 2 — From structure to energy
text:
Calculation resources
For every CRYSTAL calculation in this laboratory use:
cluminer-crystal INPUT.d12 --cores-per-node 2 --threads 2
This corresponds to one MPI rank using two OpenMP threads on two physical CPU cores. Do not request more resources unless instructed.

title: Assignment 0 — Before the first laboratory
text:
Preparation
Read the five pages under Getting Started in order.
Then complete the following checks in your own private workspace repository.

Your repository was created with Use this template → Create a new repository.
Your repository visibility is Private.
Your Codespace opens successfully.
The first environment initialization reaches Environment ready..
The Python environment passes:
python -c "import gemmi, spglib, numpy, scipy, pandas, matplotlib; print('Environment OK')"
Both update-course and start-lab are available.
You can edit and save work/SMOKE_TEST.md.
You can commit and synchronize that change with GitHub.
You can see the updated file in your repository on github.com.
You can stop the Codespace and reopen the same Codespace successfully.







NoteNo scientific work is required yet



This onboarding task only checks the working environment. The first mineral-science notebook will be introduced during Laboratory 1.


If any step fails, keep the exact error message and report it before the laboratory session.
